links.note: 1021 says no greatness has more dignity (பீடு) than that of the one who says 'I will not stay my hand' (கைதூவேன்) from the work. 611 says not to slacken at a task's difficulty because effort itself gives greatness (பெருமை முயற்சி தரும்). Both locate பெருமை in persistence rather than in rank or result; 1021 applies it to the work of raising one's family.

1021 praises the resolve never to stop work once begun (கைதூவேன்). 612 gives the other side: guard against the work dying in mid-course (வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல்), since, in Parimelazhagar's reading, the world gives up on those who give up their unfinished work. The pair shows the same refusal to stop as honour in one verse and as a condition of the world's regard in the other.

1022 says the family (குடி) lengthens through long-continued work that has both effort (ஆள்வினை) and mature knowledge. 604 states the reverse case: for those sunk in sloth, without worthy exertion (மாண்ட உஞற்றிலவர்), the family dies down and faults multiply (குடிமடிந்து குற்றம் பெருகும்). Together they make one claim from both sides: the fortunes of a குடி follow the exertion of its members.

1022 pairs effort with full knowledge (ஆள்வினையும் ஆன்ற அறிவும்) as the two things that extend a family. 618 uses the same pairing when it assigns blame: lacking fortune is no disgrace, but lacking effort after knowing what should be known (அறிவறிந்து ஆள்வினை இன்மை) is. In both verses knowledge and effort are named together as what a person can be held to, as against fortune.

1023 says that for one who resolves 'I will raise my family', தெய்வம் itself tucks up its cloth and goes in front. 619 allows that தெய்வம் may make an end unattainable (தெய்வத்தான் ஆகாதெனினும்) and promises only that effort pays the wage of the body's strain. Read together, 619 limits 1023: divine help is not guaranteed to effort in general, and 1023 claims it specifically for the one working for his குடி.

Both verses end on the phrase தான் முந்துறும், 'itself goes ahead'. In 380 it is fate (ஊழ்) that arrives first, whatever other course a person devises; in 1023 it is தெய்வம் that girds itself and goes ahead of the person who undertakes to raise his family. The shared phrase shows the same power pictured once as outrunning human plans and once as running in front to help them.

1023 has தெய்வம் tying up its garment (மடிதற்று) to go before the family-builder. 617 says the dark goddess lives in sloth (மடி) and the lotus goddess in the effort of the one without sloth (மடியிலான் தாள்). Both put divine favour on the side of the one who works; 1023's மடி (cloth) also echoes the மடி (sloth) that 617 and the chapter on sloth condemn.

The two verses share the phrase தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர், 'those who strive without delay'. 620 says such people will see even fate's back; 1024 says that for those who strive so for their family, the work reaches its end by itself without their planning it (சூழாமல் தானே முடிவெய்தும்). 1024 applies 620's general claim to the family and states its result in a stronger form.

467 says to resolve on a task only after thinking it through (எண்ணித் துணிக கருமம்), and calls thinking afterwards a lapse. 1024 says that for those who work promptly for their family the end is reached 'without deliberating' (சூழாமல்). The conflict holds on Parimelazhagar's reading, where the doer need not work out how to complete the task; Manakkudavar reads it as the result arriving before one has even thought of it, which is praise of merit rather than a rule against planning.

525 says one who gives and speaks sweetly will be surrounded by layers of kin (சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). 1025 uses the same play on சுற்றம்/சுற்றும்: the world gathers as kin (சுற்றமாச் சுற்றும் உலகு) around one who lives raising his family without fault. 1025 widens the circle from one's kin to the world and changes its cause from giving to blameless work for the குடி.

544 says the world stands embracing the feet of the king who rules embracing his people (குடிதழீஇ ... அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும் உலகு). 1025 says the world circles as kin the man who lives building up his family without fault. The same pattern appears in kingship and in the household: whoever takes care of his குடி finds the world attaching itself to him.

773 says fierceness is called great manliness (பேராண்மை), and that helping a foe in distress (ஊராண்மை) is its edge. 1026 says good manliness (நல்லாண்மை) is making oneself the one who manages the house one was born in (இல்லாண்மை). Each verse takes ஆண்மை and coins a second compound that turns it toward care for others; Parimelazhagar notes that 'நல்' in 1026 is there to set it apart from the manliness of war.

148 calls not looking at another man's wife great manliness (பேராண்மை). 1026 defines good manliness (நல்லாண்மை) as taking on the governance of one's own family. In both, the word for manly strength is given a domestic meaning: restraint in 148, responsibility in 1026.

1027 says that as in battle the load falls on the stout-hearted (வன்கண்ணர்), so among kin the burden (பொறை) falls on those able to carry it. 770 says an army has no existence without leaders, however many steady men it has (தலைமக்கள் இல்வழி இல்). 770 is the military fact that 1027 uses as its simile: numbers do not carry a force or a family, a few capable people do.

481 says kings who want to win need the right time, as the crow beats the owl only by day. 1028 says those who raise their family have no season (பருவம் இல்லை). Parimelazhagar himself cites 481 here and reads 1028 as denying that the rule of waiting for the time applies to this work, where putting it off for weather or season is only sloth (மடி).

961 tells one to give up even indispensable things if they diminish one, and its chapter places மானம் above life. 1028 says that if the family-builder idles and thinks of மானம் (மானங் கருத), the family is ruined. The conflict holds if மானம் means the same honour in both, as in Pope's rendering; Parimelazhagar narrows it in 1028 to a resentful pride ('why should I alone suffer?'), which removes the conflict.

627 says the great, knowing the body is a target for suffering (இலக்கம் உடம்பு இடும்பைக்கு), do not treat trouble as distress. 1029 asks whether the body of the man who shields his family from harm is a vessel for suffering alone (இடும்பைக்கே கொள்கலம் கொல்லோ). Both make the body the place where இடும்பை lands; 627 says it of everyone, 1029 of the one who takes on his family's troubles as well.

615 describes one who does not want pleasure but wants the work (இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான்) as the pillar who wipes away his kin's sorrows. 1029 looks at that same person from the inside: his body seems to hold nothing but suffering. 1029 states the cost of the role that 615 praises; Parimelazhagar takes the question as noting that pleasure never reaches him.

1030 says a family with no good man to stand by and prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள்) falls when trouble cuts at its foot. 615 calls the man who loves work a pillar who wipes away his kin's troubles and props them (துடைத்தூன்றும் தூண்). Both use the verb ஊன்று, to prop: 615 shows the prop in place and 1030 shows the family without it, which the commentators picture as a tree felled.

449 says those without a supporting prop (மதலையாஞ் சார்பு) have no standing (நிலை), as those without capital have no profit; it is said of a ruler who lacks great men beside him. 1030 says a family without a good man to prop it falls under trouble. The same structural image, a thing that stands only while something holds it up, is applied to a king in 449 and to a family in 1030.

1031 says the world, wherever it turns, comes behind the plough (ஏர்ப் பின்னது உலகம்), so farming is foremost. 14 says ploughmen will not plough with the plough (ஏரின் உழாஅர் உழவர்) if the rain's bounty declines. 14 puts a condition under 1031: the world depends on the plough, and the plough depends on the rain.

1032 calls those who plough the linchpin (ஆணி) of the world's people, because they carry all who go to other work. 667 says not to scorn people for their appearance, since some are like the linchpin of a great rolling chariot (அச்சாணி அன்னார்). The image is the same in both: a small part that keeps the whole vehicle from falling apart, used in 667 for the unimpressive but essential person and in 1032 for the farmer.

42 says the householder is the support (துணை) of renouncers, the destitute and the dead. 1032 says the ploughmen bear (பொறுத்து) everyone who does not plough. Both verses identify one group whose ordinary work holds up all the others: the householder in the Book of Virtue, the farmer in the Book of Wealth.

1033 says only those who plough and eat (உழுதுண்டு) truly live, while the rest eat by bowing to others. 1065 says nothing is sweeter than eating what one's own effort brought (தாள் தந்தது), even if it is thin gruel. Both value food by whether one's own labour produced it, 1033 as independence and 1065 as sweetness.

1033 describes everyone but the farmer as those who bow, eat and walk behind others (தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல்பவர்). 967 says it is better to be called ruined than to live by going behind those who do not accept one (ஒட்டார் பின்சென்று வாழ்தல்). Both treat 'going behind' another for a living as a lesser life; 967 judges it by honour, and 1033 names farming as the livelihood that avoids it.

389 says the world rests under the umbrella (கவிகை) of a king who can bear bitter words. 1034 says those who have the shade of grain will see the shade of many umbrellas come under their own umbrella (தங்குடைக்கீழ்), which Parimelazhagar takes as their own king's. Both use the royal umbrella's shade for dominion, but 389 credits the king's character and 1034 credits the farmers' harvest.

545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules justly (பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு). 1034 says those who hold the grain bring many kings' umbrellas under their own. The dependence runs in both directions: in 545 good rule yields harvest, and in 1034 harvest yields the king's wider rule.

1061 says that not begging (இரவாமை), even from those who give gladly without concealing (கரவாது), is worth ten million times more. 1035 says those whose way is to eat what their own hands produce do not beg (இரவார்) and give to askers without concealing (கரவாது ஈவர்). 1035 names the livelihood that makes the ideal of 1061 possible, and puts the farmer on the giving side of the same exchange.

613 says the proud distinction of helping others (வேளாண்மை) rests on the quality of labour (தாளாண்மை). 1035 says those who live by the work of their hands (கைசெய்தூண்) are the ones who give to those who ask. Both make giving depend on one's own labour: 613 as a principle, 1035 in the person of the cultivator.

19 says neither giving nor austerity (தானம் தவம்) will stay in the world if the sky does not give. 1036 says that if the farmers' hands fold (கைம்மடங்கின்), even those who say 'we have given up desire' cannot keep their state. Both make the ascetic life depend on a material source, the rain in 19 and the farmer in 1036, and with verse 14 they form a chain from rain to plough to renouncer.

263 asks whether the others have forgotten austerity out of a wish to provide for those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி). 1036 says that without the farmer's work the renouncer cannot hold his state (நிலை). Both say renunciation is carried by people who do not renounce; 1036 identifies the farmer as the one it finally rests on.

1037 says that if ploughed soil is dried until a measure of dust (தொடிப்புழுதி) falls to a quarter (கஃசு), the crop thrives without even a handful of manure. 1038 says manuring is better than ploughing (ஏரினும் நன்றால் எருவிடுதல்). The two set tillage and manure against each other from opposite sides: thorough working of the soil can replace manure, yet as a rule manure counts for more than ploughing.

1038 lists the stages of raising a crop, including the point after weeding (கட்டபின்), and ranks guarding above watering. 550 says a king punishing the cruel with death is like weeding the young crop (பைங்கூழ் களைகட்டதனொடு நேர்). 550 borrows for kingship one of the farmer's tasks that 1038 gives literally; in both, removing what harms the crop is part of tending it.

1038 treats manure (எரு) and water (நீர்) as what makes a crop grow. In 1147 the woman says her love-sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and her mother's words as water (கெளவை எருவாக அன்னைசொல் நீராக). The Book of Love takes the two inputs that 1038 gives as farming advice and uses them as a figure for what feeds her passion.

1039 says that if the owner (கிழவன்) stays away and does not go to it, the land turns against him and sulks like a wife. 553 says the king who does not look into things and do justice every day loses his land day by day (நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்). In both, land is lost through the owner's or ruler's lack of personal attention; Parimelazhagar reads 1039 too as requiring a daily visit.

1039 describes neglected land with the Book of Love's words for a lovers' sulk: it resents and sulks like a wife (புலந்து ... ஊடி விடும்). 1304, in the chapter on sulking, says that not appeasing one who has sulked (ஊடியவரை உணராமை) is like cutting a withered creeper at the root. The figures run in opposite directions: the land is compared to a sulking woman in 1039, and the neglected sulking woman to a plant in 1304.

1039 compares the land to a wife (இல்லாள்) who sulks when her owner stays away. 1040 calls the land a good woman (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள்) who laughs at those who sit idle pleading poverty. The chapter closes with two verses that make the land a woman who responds to how a man treats her, by sulking in one and by laughing in the other.

271 says the five elements laugh inwardly (அகத்தே நகும்) at the false conduct of the deceitful-minded. 1040 says the good woman called Land laughs (நகும்) on seeing those who say 'we have nothing' and sit idle. In both verses a part of the natural world laughs at a person's self-deception; Parimelazhagar adds that the Land too laughs to herself.

205 says not to do evil on the plea 'I have nothing' (இலன் என்று), because doing so makes one poor again. 1040 has the Land laugh at those who say 'we have nothing' (இலமென்று) and sit idle. The same plea of poverty is rejected as an excuse in both, for wrongdoing in 205 and for idleness in 1040.

616 says effort creates prosperity and lack of effort brings in want (முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்திவிடும்). 1040 pictures the Land laughing at people who claim poverty while sitting idle (அசைஇ இருப்பார்). Both hold that such poverty comes from not working; 1040 states it as mockery from the land that would have paid them.
